To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) “drug-likeness” is a function of the molecular weight, lipophilic efficiency, and number of hydrogen bond acceptors; 2) the most important structural feature of drug binding sites is the number of hydrogen bond donors; 3) the most druggable targets are enzymes; 4) the least druggable targets tend to be receptors, ion channels and transporters; 5) the best targets are enzymes with high ligand efficiency, low molecular weight

(1) the physicochemical properties of drug-like molecules are defined; (2) a method for assessing target druggability has been established; and (3) this target analysis has been applied to the human proteome.

“the druggability of a target can only be assessed by a detailed, multi-disciplinary analysis of all the information available, which can then be combined with a detailed understanding of the physico-chemical basis of drug-like molecules to provide a quantitative assessment of the druggability of the target”.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification and analysis of protein targets for drug discovery.

(a) the development of methods to assess the “druggabilty” of a protein target, and (b) the development of computational approaches that can be used to identify “drug-like” small molecules that bind to these targets.
the development of computational methods for target assessment and drug design.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
“druggability is a function of the structural and thermodynamics basis of protein-lipand interactions”.
“Target analysis is a key tool for target validation”.
the target analysis process can provide a powerful tool for prioritising targets, but it is not a panacea for drug design.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
“druggability is a function of target sequence and structure, ligand binding thermodynamics and ligand properties”.
the “druggable genome” is about 10% of all genes.
the druggability of the human proteome is 10-15% and that the majority of the druggable proteome can be targeted by small molecules.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the “druggable genome” is much smaller than has previously been appreciated.
target assessment is a powerful tool to help prioritize drug discovery projects, and that there are a number of simple and robust methods to assess druggability.
target analysis can be used to identify targets that are “druggable”, and those that are not.
